I don't think people even understand what martial law is. In martial law the military takes over and replaces civilian leadership, including the president and congress. I've had the experience of living in countries under martial law and it typically used as an anti-political tool. In particular when the civilians prove irreconcilably corrupt or incapable of competent leadership martial law may be imposed in order to reorganize the government.

The first step is that political leaders would be deposed. The president doesn't make a speech - the president is gone under martial law. After that, television/radio/internet broadcasts would likely inform the people of what has happened and what the goals are. Their goals would likely be to restore order, if chaos had broken out, and to schedule a new election for all new provisional representatives. Curfews, checkpoints, rules prohibiting gatherings and so on would likely only be used in cases where there was already an active insurrection.

From a day to day point of view there'd be minimal change. The big difference is you'd have military leadership in charge of public institutions, budgeting, and so on until a new civilian government could be formed.
The President would not be gone in the US because he is the Commander and Chief of the Military, but congress would.

There are numerous civilian roles at the head of all military branches, for instance the Secretary of the Navy is the chief of the navy. However, martial law is law by commissioned military - civilian titles, regardless of their relationship to the military, are irrelevant.
The president/governor would mobilize the military/national guard, and people would have to do as they are told.

There are, however, other costs in the budget that should be lumped under the rubric of national defense. For starters, there is about $33 billion in the non-Pentagon portion of what is official classified as “national defense.” Aside from the Pentagon and the wars, that includes the cost of the nation’s nuclear weapons (chiefly within the Department of Energy), and some mandatory spending not captured in the DoD base budget and OCO figures shown above. That brings requested defense spending to $647.4 billion. In addition, as Winslow Wheeler of the Center for Defense Information points out, the Obama administration has requested $137.7 billion for Veterans Affairs, and $46 billion for homeland security (that’s a government-wide total compiled by the Office and Management and Budget, excluding the defense portion). Wheeler also points to another $29.4 billion in military retirement and DoD retiree health care costs (these show up under budget functions 550, 650, and 950).
